title: Virtue Ethics and Eastern Traditions
welcome_lead: From Aristotle's flourishing to Buddhist skilful means and Confucian relationships — compare virtue-based ethics.
meta_desc: Religious Studies Adventure: virtue ethics, Buddhist ethics and Confucianism.
final_note: You have walked the paths of cultivated character. Virtue traditions remain vital across religions.

concepts.def: Aristotle's notion of human flourishing as the highest good achieved through virtuous activity.
Aristotle's principle that virtue lies between excess and deficiency, e.g. courage between cowardice and rashness.
Buddhist concept of teaching and acting in ways appropriate to context and capacity.
Confucian virtue of humaneness or benevolence, central to ethical life.

walkthroughs.body_html: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics grounds ethics in the cultivation of character traits — phronesis (practical wisdom), justice, courage, temperance — that enable eudaimonia. Virtues are habituated dispositions reached through practice and education.

Buddhist ethics emphasises sila (moral conduct), karuna (compassion) and metta (loving-kindness). The Five Precepts cover non-harming, non-stealing, sexual responsibility, truthful speech and abstaining from intoxicants. Upaya recognises that ethical action must adapt to context to relieve suffering.

Confucian ethics centres on cultivating ren and li within the five relationships (ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger sibling, friend-friend). Sikh ethics emphasises selfless service (seva), honest livelihood, sharing with the community and devotion to one God, articulated through the Guru Granth Sahib.
